title: Spared by the feet that humbled him
hookLine: the serpent's wives plead for his life, and the marks of Krishna's feet become his protection
carry: his lotus feet humble, then protect
tomorrow: Why the village fed a hill

lines: HIS WIVES COME OUT OF THE POOL.
cards: The serpent is beaten. He lies broken in the water, the boy still standing on his heads. And out of the pool come the serpent's wives.
The Bhagavata calls them the naga wives, and they don't come to fight. They come with their children in front of them, hair loose, clothes disordered, and bow before Krishna with their palms joined.
Kaliya can't speak for himself anymore. So they speak for him.

teach.b: What they say is surprising. They don't argue that their husband is innocent. They call his punishment fair, more than fair: a grace.
Your feet have touched his head, they say, and others perform long austerities hoping for the dust of those feet. Then they ask one thing: spare him. He is our husband.
Let him live. And Krishna lets him go. Kaliya, getting his breath back, speaks plainly.
We serpents are born this way, angry by nature, with poison in us. It's hard to let go of what you're made of.

teach.h: GO TO THE OCEAN; LET THE RIVER BE CLEAN.
teach.b: Krishna gives him a way forward: leave this pool, go to the ocean with your family, so the river can be clean again for the people and the cows. Then Krishna names the fear that brought Kaliya here. He was hiding.
Garuda, the eagle who preys on serpents, could not enter this pool because of a sage's old curse, so this poisoned corner of the Yamuna was the one place he felt safe. And Krishna answers that fear.

Garuda won't harm you now, he says, because you carry the marks of my feet on your hoods. So the story ends with no one destroyed. The poison leaves the river, and the feet that broke his pride become his shelter.

That's why Hindu devotion speaks so often of the Lord's lotus feet. People bow at the feet of the image in the temple. Many temples give charanamrit, water that has bathed the deity's feet, as a blessing.
To take refuge at his feet, as devotees say, means this: what humbles you is also what keeps you safe.

how: Devotees retell the prayer of Kaliya's wives as a model of surrender, and in some depictions of Kaliya-mardana the naga wives are shown with joined palms beside the serpent.

o: the sage whose curse kept Garuda from the pool
the serpent spared, protected by the marks of his feet
the naga queen who pleads for her husband's life

s: Kaliya's wives say he was innocent
they call his punishment fair, even a grace, and ask only for his life.
Kaliya was hiding in the pool from Garuda
a sage's curse kept Garuda out of that pool.
Krishna's footprints on the hoods protect Kaliya afterward
Garuda won't harm the serpent who bears them.

games.q: you're at a temple. people around you bow low at the feet of Krishna's image. why the feet?
o: the face is too holy to look at.
his feet are refuge: the feet that humbled Kaliya then kept him safe.
they're just the easiest part to reach.
games.why: Kaliya's hoods carried the marks of Krishna's feet, and Garuda couldn't harm him. devotees take refuge at the lotus feet.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose sharpness you've felt, and gently wonder what they might be afraid of, what corner they crawled into to feel safe.

If you pray, picture laying them at Krishna's feet, the way Kaliya's wives did, and asking that they be spared, and sent somewhere better than their poison. If you don't pray, simply wish them a cleaner river to live in.

wordCard.voice: Kaliya. The serpent spared at his wives' plea, sent to the ocean, and protected by the very footprints that subdued him.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Garuda, the great eagle, the bird Kaliya feared.
